# Summary: 1997 Conservative Party Manifesto

The Conservative Party presents itself as the architect of Britain's transformation from "the sick man of Europe" to its most successful economy. Since 1979, Conservative administrations have liberated British enterprise from excessive state control, tamed over-mighty trade unions, and restored economic prosperity through free-market principles.

## Economic Achievement and Vision

Britain has achieved remarkable success: inflation at historic lows, unemployment falling while rising across Europe, the lowest tax burden of any major European economy, and record inward investment. The party's goal is to make Britain "the Enterprise Centre of Europe" by continuing tight control of public spending, working towards a 20p basic rate of income tax, and maintaining inflation at 2.5% or below. The manifesto explicitly rejects the failing "European social model" of high regulation and burdensome costs on business.

## Opportunity and Family

Conservatives believe families, not governments, should make decisions. The party proposes tax reforms allowing families to transfer unused personal allowances between spouses when caring for children or dependents. A revolutionary pension scheme would give young workers personal pension funds through national insurance rebates, creating genuine independence from state dependency. The right to buy has already created 1.5 million new homeowners; further expansion of ownership across shares, homes, and savings will continue.

## Public Services and Health

The NHS will receive continued real-terms funding increases. Reforms have enabled hospitals and GP practices to run their own affairs, treating over one million more patients annually. The party proposes extended fundholding for GPs, primary care expansion, and private sector partnerships to modernise facilities—delivering better services without Labour's command-and-control approach.

## Law and Order

Crime has fallen for four consecutive years under Conservative stewardship. The manifesto pledges continued investment in police, 10,000 CCTV cameras, mandatory minimum sentences for persistent offenders, and tackling juvenile crime through swift sanctions and parental responsibility orders. Prison works—keeping criminals off streets protects the public.

## Europe and National Sovereignty

Britain must be "in Europe but not run by Europe." The Conservatives secured the Social Chapter opt-out, protecting British businesses from costly regulation. A federal European state is rejected absolutely. Any decision to join a single currency would require a referendum, though current convergence makes joining in 1999 highly unlikely. National parliaments must retain supremacy over European institutions.

## The Union and Constitution

The Union between Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and England provides essential stability. Devolution would create dangerous strains risking the break-up of the United Kingdom. Constitutional evolution—not revolution—protects British freedoms better than abstract bills of rights that would transfer power to unelected judges.

## The Choice

Voters face a stark choice: continue the path of enterprise, low taxation, and national sovereignty that has restored Britain's prosperity, or risk everything by handing power to Labour—who opposed every reform and would burden Britain with new spending, taxation, and regulation while surrendering sovereignty to Europe.

**"You can only be sure with the Conservatives."**
